free_tier.stated: No storage quota of its own — it is a *serving and permanence* layer over npm and GitHub, so the quota is whatever the origin package holds. Hard limits: packages >150 MB and (for GitHub) single files >20 MB are refused by default, raisable on request.
free_tier.notes: the headline offer as the seed recorded it; the binding constraint is in limits[]

per_object_cap.notes: extracted from the quota or limits prose

retention.stated: | Retention is *stronger* than the origin: 'Previously served immutable files may be retained in permanent storage even after upstream deletion

egress.terms: Fully free and explicitly unmetered. Terms of Use (effective Oct 5, 2026), verbatim: 'using jsDelivr CDN is free for both personal and commercial use, there are no limits on bandwidth or number of requests.' About page: 'There are no bandwidth limits or premium features and its completely free to use by anybody.'

tooling: Plain GET on cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/<pkg>@<ver>/<path> and /gh/<owner>/<repo>@<ref>/<path>. No client needed. Cache-purge API exists (email-gated).
chaining: Chains onto npm (see npm candidate) or onto GitHub repos: publish the blob as an npm tarball, then serve it from jsDelivr at a URL with 1-year immutable cache and no bandwidth charge. This upgrades any npm/GitHub bulk store from 'downloadable' to 'CDN-served with free egress', which is exactly the 1 TiB/day serving workload.
limits_note: 150 MB per npm package, 20 MB per single GitHub file (both default, raisable via GitHub issue). Rate limiting applies to purge, not to reads. Terms prohibit 'using jsDelivr CDN as a general-purpose file or media hosting service' and 'hosting videos, file backups, or other files in large quantities' — enforcement is the technical risk, not the capability.

identity_cost.detail: no identity_cost field and no identity statement in the source record; defaulted to email and flagged, not evidence

reliability_note: Retention is *stronger* than the origin: 'Previously served immutable files may be retained in permanent storage even after upstream deletion. We do not accept removal requests simply because a package or version was unpublished, deleted upstream, or is no longer needed.' Once a URL has been fetched it keeps working after you delete the npm package — that is a genuine cold-archive property. Counter-risk: a 150 MB package cap means a naive >150 MB npm tarball 403s ('Package size exceeded the configured limit of 150 MB') even though npm itself accepted it.
